tips.title: Plants for phyto, bacteria for bio
tips.body: **Phyto**mining uses **plants** — *phyto* means plant. **Bio**leaching uses **bacteria**. The names carry the answer, and mixing them up is the commonest error in this topic.

tips.title: Ash from plants, leachate from bacteria
tips.body: Phytomining harvests the plants and **burns** them to give **ash** containing metal compounds. Bioleaching gives a **leachate solution** containing metal compounds. One is a solid, one is a solution — and questions ask which.

tips.title: Both give a compound, not the metal
tips.body: Neither method produces copper directly. Both end with a **copper compound**, which then has to be processed by **displacement with scrap iron** or by **electrolysis**. An answer that stops at the ash or the leachate has not finished.

tips.title: Why scrap iron works
tips.body: Iron is **more reactive** than copper, so it **displaces** copper from a solution of its compounds. Using **scrap** iron makes it cheap, which matters when the copper is this dilute.

tips.title: The point is low-grade ore
tips.body: These methods exist because **copper ores are becoming scarce** and what is left is **low grade**. Traditional mining would mean digging, moving and disposing of huge amounts of rock for very little metal — so the comparison is always against that.

why.matters:
The easy copper has been dug up. What is left is **low-grade ore** — rock with a very small percentage of copper in it — and moving a hillside to get a few kilograms is not worth doing, whatever the price.

So the alternatives change the problem instead of the chemistry. A plant or a bacterium does the concentrating, slowly and cheaply and over a whole field, and only then does anyone bother with a reaction. The metal is won at the end by exactly the methods you already know.

examples.title: Growing a crop to mine copper
examples.body:
Phytomining is farming for metal. Plants are grown on land with copper compounds in it — spoil heaps, or ground too poor to mine — and as they grow they **absorb the compounds through their roots** and concentrate them in their tissue.

Then the crop is harvested and **burned**, and the ash contains far more copper per kilogram than the ground ever did. The plant has done the digging, the sorting and the concentrating, using sunlight, on land that was already spoiled.

visual.alt: A flow chart of phytomining: plants are grown on low-grade ground, absorb the copper compounds, are harvested and burned, and the ash that is left is rich in copper compounds rather than in copper itself

examples.title: Plants for phyto, bacteria for bio
examples.body:
The two methods are easy to mix up and the names carry the answer. **Phyto**mining uses **plants**; **bio**leaching uses **bacteria** grown on the ore, whose metabolism breaks it down and washes the copper out into solution.

What matters more is what each one leaves you with. Phytomining gives **ash**, a solid. Bioleaching gives a **leachate**, a solution. Neither gives copper — both give copper compounds, and an answer that stops at the ash has stopped one step early.

visual.alt: A table of the two biological extraction methods: phytomining uses plants and leaves ash, bioleaching uses bacteria and leaves a leachate solution, and both leave copper compounds rather than copper

examples.title: Finishing the job with scrap iron
examples.body:
The copper still has to come out of its compound, and the cheapest way is a reaction from Year 9: **iron is more reactive than copper**, so it displaces it from a solution of its salt.

Using **scrap** iron makes it cheaper still, which matters when the copper is this dilute — the iron is waste and the copper drops out as a solid you can filter off. Electrolysis is the other option, and it gives purer copper, but it is the expensive one for the same reason aluminium is expensive.

equations.name: Displacement with scrap iron
equations.units: iron is above copper, so it takes its place

visual.alt: The equation for displacing copper with scrap iron: iron plus copper sulfate gives iron sulfate and copper, because iron is higher in the reactivity series

steps.title: Why new methods are needed
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

The Earth's resources of **metal ores are limited**, and the richest deposits get used first. **Copper ores are becoming scarce**, and what remains is mostly **low grade** — rock containing only a small percentage of copper.

**The problem with traditional mining.** Getting copper the ordinary way means **digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock**. With a high-grade ore that is worth doing. With a low-grade ore the same effort yields far less metal, so the cost per tonne of copper rises sharply — and so does the environmental damage, because the quarry, the waste rock and the energy used are much the same either way.

A tonne of ore at $2\%$ copper yields $20\text{ kg}$; at $0.4\%$ it yields only $4\text{ kg}$ — **5 times less** for the same hole in the ground.

**Two biological alternatives** let low-grade ores be worked without the digging: **phytomining** and **bioleaching**. Both use living organisms to concentrate the copper, and both **avoid the traditional mining methods** of moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.

steps.title: Phytomining
steps.body:
**Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds.**

1. Plants are grown on soil or spoil containing **low concentrations** of copper compounds.
2. As they grow, the plants **absorb the metal compounds** through their roots and concentrate them in their tissue.
3. The plants are **harvested** and then **burned**.
4. Burning produces **ash that contains the metal compounds**, now far more concentrated than in the original rock.
5. The copper is then obtained from the ash by **displacement** or **electrolysis**.

**Why it helps.** The plants do the concentrating, so no rock has to be dug out and moved. The land can be low-grade spoil left over from earlier mining, which is otherwise useless.

**The drawbacks.** It is **slow** — plants take a growing season, so the copper comes out over years rather than weeks. It depends on **climate and land**, and the yield per hectare is small.

**A useful detail**: burning the plants releases the energy stored in them, which can be captured, and the ash is a much richer source of copper than any ore.

steps.title: Bioleaching
steps.body:
**Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.**

1. Bacteria are grown on the **low-grade ore**.
2. Their metabolism **breaks down the ore**, releasing the copper into solution.
3. The result is a **leachate** — a solution containing **copper compounds**.
4. The copper is obtained from the leachate by **displacement** or **electrolysis**.

**Why it helps.** Like phytomining, it works on ore too poor for traditional extraction, and it avoids the large-scale digging and rock disposal.

**The drawbacks.** It is also **slow**. It can produce **toxic substances**, including sulfuric acid, which damage the local environment if they escape — so the leachate has to be contained and treated.

**Comparing the two.** Both are **slow** but **low-energy** compared with smelting, and both work on ores that would otherwise be waste. Phytomining needs **land and a growing season**; bioleaching needs the **ore itself** and careful containment of the leachate.

**Neither gives copper directly** — both give a **copper compound** that still has to be processed.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Finish the process.** Phytomining gives **ash**; bioleaching gives a **leachate**. Both contain **copper compounds**, not copper. The answer is only complete once you have added displacement with scrap iron or electrolysis.

**Name the organism precisely.** Plants for phytomining, bacteria for bioleaching. "Living things" is not enough.

**Compare against traditional mining, not against nothing.** The advantage is that these methods work on **low-grade ore** and avoid **digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock**. That phrase is straight from the specification and earns the mark.

**Give the drawbacks honestly.** Both are **slow**. Bioleaching can produce **toxic substances** including sulfuric acid. Phytomining needs **land, a suitable climate and a growing season**. A one-sided answer caps below the top band.

**Justify scrap iron by reactivity and cost.** Iron is **above copper** in the reactivity series, so it displaces it; using **scrap** keeps the cost down, which matters because the copper is so dilute.

**Explain the electrolysis electrode.** Copper ions are **positive**, so they are attracted to the **negative** electrode, where they gain electrons and are deposited as copper metal.

**Link to sustainability.** These methods conserve a **finite** resource by making previously uneconomic deposits usable, and they use **less energy** than smelting. That is the connection to the wider unit.

**Read the data in an evaluation question.** If figures are given for yield, time and energy, quote them. A judgement supported by numbers beats one supported by adjectives.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- *(Higher tier only.)* The Earth's **metal ores are limited**, and **copper ores are becoming scarce**.
- Remaining deposits are **low grade**, so traditional mining moves huge amounts of rock for little metal.
- **Phytomining** uses **plants**: they absorb metal compounds, are **harvested and burned**, and the **ash contains metal compounds**.
- **Bioleaching** uses **bacteria**: they produce a **leachate solution** containing metal compounds.
- Both **avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock**.
- Both are **slow**; bioleaching can produce **toxic substances**.
- Neither gives the metal directly — both give a **compound**.
- The metal is then obtained by **displacement using scrap iron** or **electrolysis**.
- Iron displaces copper because **iron is more reactive**: $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CuSO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSO_4} + \mathrm{Cu}$.
- **Scrap** iron is used because it is **cheap**.
- In electrolysis, copper is deposited at the **negative electrode**, because copper ions are positive.
- These methods conserve a **finite resource** and use **less energy** than smelting.

questions.prompt:
A mining company owns a large deposit of copper ore containing only 0.3% copper. Traditional extraction would be uneconomic.

Describe how phytomining and bioleaching could be used to obtain copper from this deposit, and evaluate their use compared with traditional mining. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
In **phytomining**, plants are grown on the low-grade deposit. As they grow they **absorb copper compounds** through their roots and concentrate them in their tissue. The plants are then **harvested and burned**, and the **ash contains the copper compounds** in a far richer form than the original rock.

In **bioleaching**, **bacteria** are grown on the ore. Their metabolism breaks the ore down and releases the copper into a **leachate solution containing copper compounds**.

Neither route gives copper metal directly. In both cases the copper is still combined, so it must be obtained from its compounds either by **displacement using scrap iron** — iron is more reactive than copper, so $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CuSO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSO_4} + \mathrm{Cu}$, and scrap keeps the cost low — or by **electrolysis**, which deposits very pure copper at the negative electrode but uses a great deal of electrical energy.

**Against traditional mining**, the great advantage is that both work on ore containing only $0.3\%$ copper, which would never repay conventional extraction. They **avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock**, so the landscape damage and the waste heaps are far smaller, and they use **less energy** than smelting.

**Against that**, both are **slow** — phytomining needs a growing season for each crop — and bioleaching can produce **toxic substances** such as sulfuric acid that must be contained. For a deposit this poor, traditional mining is not a realistic option at all, so the choice is between the two biological routes: phytomining if the site has suitable land and climate, bioleaching if it does not and the leachate can be safely contained.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the organism for each method, states the intermediate correctly — ash for phytomining, leachate for bioleaching — and always finishes the process with displacement or electrolysis, justifying scrap iron by reactivity and cost.
